fetched_contents.text: Gravity currents produced by lock-release: Theory and experiments concerning the effect of a free top in non-Boussinesq systems Introduction Classical models of gravity currents (GCs) typically envisage a GC produced by lock-release advancing in an ambient fluid while the two-fluid system is contained from above by a fixed boundary (see (Ungarish, 2009) and the references therein). In most analyses the density of the current ρ1 is slightly different from the ambient fluid’s ρ2, hence the ratio r=ρ2/ρ1≈1. This is the Boussinesq case whereas the condition r < 0.9 is defined as the non-Boussinesq case. The lock released GC in a channel of rectangular cross-section with a fixed top in non-Boussinesq conditions has been studied experimentally, numerically and analitically (Birman, Martin, Meiburg, 2005, Bonometti, Balachandar, Magnaudet, 2008, Bonometti, Ungarish, Balachandar, 2011, Dai, 2014, Étienne, Hopfinger, Saramito, 2005, Gröbelbauer, Fanneløp, Britter, 1993, Jacobson, Testik, 2013, Lowe, Rottman, Linden, 2005, Rotunno, Klemp, Bryan, Muraki, 2011, Turnbull, McElwaine, 2008, Ungarish, 2007, Ungarish, 2011). We emphasize that these studies are relevant to systems with a fixed-top boundary. However, in several real cases and especially in natural environments, GCs develop in an ambient fluid with a free surface, often in the presence of free surface waves see, e.g., Robinson, Eames, Simons, 2013, Stancanelli, Musumeci, Foti, 2018 or of an imposed or generated flux (Longo, Ungarish, Di Federico, Chiapponi, Addona, 2016, Taghavi, Seon, Martinez, Frigaard, 2010). The effect of the open boundary on the motion of the lock-released (or lock-exchange) GC is a relatively uninvestigated topic. The presence of the open surface introduces a significant complication in the analysis of the GC, because the height of the upper boundary is now a variable of distance x and time t, which must be calculated (or measured in the laboratory). Moreover, the deviation from the fixed-top case turns out to be proportional to (1−r), and hence a reliable investigation must cover the more complex non-Boussinesq regime. This lack of knowledge has motivated the present investigation. The present paper attempts to clarify, and model, some salient effects of the GC system with an open surface. The progress in the understanding of the GC with fixed top has been strongly facilitated by the availability of the classical Benjamin (1968) solution which is valid for both Boussinesq and non-Boussinesq systems with fixed top. Benjamin’s speed and dissipation formulas serve as essential components in shallow-water models and in the interpretation of simulation and laboratory data. On the other hand, no counterpart solution was available for the free-surface systems until recently. A recent paper by Ungarish (2017) has demonstrated that the classical (Benjamin, 1968) solution can be extended to solve the free surface case, with a new front condition. Qualitatively, the open-surface problem introduces a decrease effect, or depression, χ in the height of the ambient fluid H, as a footprint of the advancing nose of the current. Since the ratio χ/H is proportional to Δρ/ρ2, (Δρ=ρ1−ρ2), in Boussinesq conditions the effect is small and usually neglected (with little or no comment). For non-Boussinesq conditions, the depression can be relevant and, to higher orders, interferes with the GC front speed and height. Experimental data for open surface systems are available, but only for Boussinesq systems, with the exception of very recent experiments reported in Sciortino et al. (2018). On the other hand, most of the shallow water (SW) two-layer results are for covered channel (for the one-layer, very deep current, the presence/absence of the cover is insignificant). Some SW two-layer open-surface results have been presented by Adduce et al. (2011), but (i) they are in the Boussinesq domain; and (ii) use an ad-hoc adjustment for the front condition, not a jump relationship. A front condition for the open-top non-Boussinesq gravity current was also suggested by Sciortino et al. (2018). This result is based on a weak-solution Rankine-Hugoniot derivation, which, in contrast to Benjamin and Ungarish (2017), does not satisfy rigorously flow-force equilibrium, energy dissipation validity, and sub-critical speed propagation; and hence it is mostly of academic value. Sciortino et al. (2018) performed accurate experiments for full-depth release currents with open surface in the non-Boussinesq regime 0.6 ≤ r ≤ 0.86. They reported reduction of speed of propagation accompanied by a depression of the surface; both effects are more enhanced as r decreases. Unfortunately they did not consider partial-depth release systems, and did not compare with time-dependent solutions of the lock-release problem. To our knowledge, Navier-Stokes simulations for this problem are also unavailable. In the present paper, we advance existing knowledge on GCs by: (i) developing a new two-layer SW model for the non-Boussinesq case; (ii) solving numerically the resulting lock-release problem; (iii) validating the numerical results with experiments; (iv) comparing SW and experimental results with a more complex Computational Fluid Dynamics code (CFD). many astrophysical scales, from sub-pc filaments in the interstellar medium to Mpc scale streams feeding galaxies from the cosmic web. These filaments are often subject to Kelvin–Helmholtz Instability (KHI) due to shearing against a confining background medium. We study the non-linear evolution of KHI in pressure-confined self-gravitating gas streams initially in hydrostatic equilibrium, using analytic models and hydrodynamic simulations, not including radiative cooling. We derive a critical line mass, or mass per unit length, as a function of the stream Mach number and density contrast with respect to the background, μcr(Mb, δc) ≤ 1, where μ = 1 is normalized to the maximal line mass for which initial hydrostatic equilibrium is possible. For μ < μcr, KHI dominates the stream evolution. A turbulent shear layer expands into the background and leads to stream deceleration at a similar rate to the non-gravitating case. However, with gravity, penetration of the shear layer into the stream is halted at roughly half the initial stream radius by stabilizing buoyancy forces, significantly delaying total stream disruption. Streams with μcr < μ ≤ 1 fragment and form round, long-lived clumps by gravitational instability (GI), with typical separations roughly eight times the stream radius, similar to the case without KHI. When KHI is still somewhat effective, these clumps are below the spherical Jeans mass and are partially confined by external pressure, but they approach the Jeans mass as μ → 1 and GI dominates. Submission received: 9 February 2025 / Revised: 25 March 2025 / Accepted: 1 April 2025 / Published: 3 April 2025 Abstract When a gravity current encounters a barrier, it is reflected as a moving hydraulic jump or bore. These reflected flows, which play a significant role in estuarine mixing and sediment transport, are often simplified in theoretical models as purely advective processes with no mixing and dilution effects. This study explores the dynamics of gravity currents fully blocked by various inclined barriers, focusing on the resulting mixing behavior. Using an image analysis technique based on light attenuation to capture instantaneous density fields, we reveal how the presence of a barrier influences the current even before impact. By applying the Thorpe scale to assess turbulent mixing, we show that a barrier’s geometry significantly affects mixing intensity. Notably, this study finds that barriers can increase the local turbulent mixing compared to horizontal surfaces. 1. Introduction Gravity currents are buoyancy-driven flows caused by variations in density due to differences in salinity, temperature, or suspended particle concentration. These currents are pivotal in shaping atmospheric, oceanic, and coastal circulations [1]. Beyond their central role in geophysical studies, gravity currents are of significant interest in engineering, particularly in applications related to industrial safety and ecosystem protection [2,3,4]. A defining characteristic of gravity currents is their interaction with complex terrains, including rough or mobile sediment beds, which can substantially alter their dynamics and influence the flow’s behavior and properties [5,6,7,8]. Recent advancements have highlighted the intricate behavior of gravity currents as they propagate through complex topographies [9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16]. When encountering obstacles, the dynamics of these flows are profoundly influenced by unsteady processes, particularly during the initial impact phase. This phase often generates the largest forces and moments acting on the structure. Despite its significance, much of the existing research has focused on the forward motion and overflow dynamics of gravity currents, leaving the reflected flows generated by obstacle interactions relatively understudied [17,18,19]. Early theoretical and experimental investigations, such as those by [20,21,22], approached this problem using shallow-water models. Driven by the need to designing barriers for hazardous dense gases, these studies introduced simplified models to estimate the correlation between obstacle height and the proportion of the incoming current that surpassed the barrier. Subsequent research by [23] employed both numerical and experimental approaches to examine the initial stages of gravity current interaction with cylindrical structures. Their work identified three distinct phases: an impact phase, a transient oscillatory phase, and a quasi-steady phase. Despite these advancements, the dynamics of reflected flows remain poorly understood. These flows are often assumed to exhibit properties analogous to the forward-moving current, with simplified models treating them as purely advective processes that neglect mixing and dilution [22,24,25]. However, experimental observations suggest that reflected flows exhibit significantly more complex behavior, particularly when interacting with low-angled ramps and other obstacles [17,26]. The mixing phenomena generated by these interactions are crucial to understanding gravity current dynamics. Mixing processes are inherently variable, influenced by factors such as the mechanisms driving turbulence, the stage of turbulent evolution, and spatial heterogeneity within the domain. Laboratory and numerical studies consistently highlight the complexity and variability of mixing, with notable contributions from [27,28,29,30,31]. However, quantifying the extent and nature of mixing remains a significant challenge due to the intricate interplay of these factors. In hydraulic theory, internal bores generated by the interaction between gravity currents and topography are often idealized as abrupt, moving jumps at the interface between immiscible fluids (e.g., [17,32]). In real-world conditions, particularly in miscible fluid systems, such idealizations fail to capture the nuances of bore structures. For instance, Ref. [33] demonstrated that internal bores with small depth changes produce insufficient shear stress and interfacial slopes to drive the substantial entrainment of ambient fluid. This highlights the limitations of hydraulic theory in describing the dynamics of mixing and entrainment under realistic conditions, emphasizing the need for experimental investigations to unravel the complexities of gravity current interactions. While previous studies have provided valuable insights into the behavior of gravity currents interacting with topographic features, the quantitative characterization of turbulence and mixing intensity near obstacles remains an open challenge. Earlier research primarily relied on qualitative observations and limited quantitative measurements, often lacking high-resolution data to assess localized turbulence generation. In this context, the present study delves into the reflection process of gravity currents as they interact with barriers. Experimental methods for observing and quantifying spreading behavior in free-surface gravity currents are typically centered on controlled tank setups and high-resolution measurement techniques. The most common apparatus configurations in the cited literature are lock-release experiments in rectangular or channel-like geometries, with a free surface or open boundary rather than a fixed lid [N1-F1]. These setups are widely used because they mimic natural and industrial flows where a less-dense fluid advances into a denser ambient, and they allow the free surface to evolve dynamically [N1-R1][N1-R2]. A recent setup also explicitly mentions a gravity-current configuration operating at inflow Reynolds numbers around 4000, using different fluids to generate the current [N1-R4]. Another cited study emphasizes the use of a free-surface system with an open boundary, which is especially relevant for less-dense-over-denser flows [N1-F1].

For velocity measurement, the evidence points to a combination of high-resolution velocity and density measurements, and in some cases, high-fidelity numerical simulations that complement laboratory experiments [N6-R3][N6-R5]. These methods are especially useful for capturing the time-dependent evolution of flows that are otherwise difficult to measure directly [N6-R3]. In the spreading-length context, the cited work on gravity currents also discusses the measurement of buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, dissolution flux, and interface length and width as observables that help characterize spreading and mixing [N2-R3]. For length scales, the evidence includes the study of spreading and leveling gravity currents in a Hele-Shaw cell, which is an analog for flows in fractures and other narrow geometries [N2-R1]. That same study suggests that spreading behavior is analyzed through spatially varying length and shape characteristics [N2-R1].

Thickness is usually inferred from the vertical extent of the current or from the interface between the two fluids. The cited gravity-current paper specifically notes that accurate measurements of the space- and time-varying free surface depression are used in experiments, which is a proxy for current height and thickness [N1-F1]. It also mentions the detection of a bounded wave following the front, which helps validate models of the current’s vertical structure [N1-F1]. In related work, the propagation of planar gravity currents into a stratified ambient is studied using direct numerical simulations and compared with high-fidelity simulation data, with attention to how internal gravity waves interact with the current head and modify its shape [N4-F4]. This indicates that thickness is often connected to the current’s head and the ambient stratification it encounters [N4-F4].

The free surface is tracked through imaging or sensor-based observation. The cited experiments explicitly use image analysis to capture instantaneous density fields, and they use light attenuation to visualize density variations [N5-F2]. This is a direct way to track the free surface and the interface between fluids. The same paper also notes that non-intrusive techniques are used to capture density fields, which is important because intrusive sensors can perturb the flow [N5-F2]. In the open-surface gravity-current context, experiments are described as measuring the free surface depression modulated by the advancing current, including the detection of bounded waves [N1-F1]. The cited study on reflected gravity currents also emphasizes image analysis as a method to reveal how barriers influence the current before impact [N5-F2]. This shows that imaging is not just a qualitative tool but a quantitative one, enabling the tracking of both surface position and density structure.

Overall, the common experimental toolkit is thus: lock-release or lock-exchange tanks with open or free-surface boundaries, high-resolution velocity and density measurements, imaging of density fields or light attenuation, and sometimes direct numerical simulations to compare with laboratory data [N1-F1][N1-R1][N6-R3][N5-F2]. These methods together allow researchers to quantify spreading speed, thickness, length scale, and free-surface evolution in free-surface gravity currents [N2-R1][N4-F4].

In less-dense-over-denser currents, the main instability modes observed experimentally are Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and Rayleigh-Taylor instability, with the latter becoming especially relevant when the background fluid is denser than the current [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The cited review and fetch material explain that Kelvin-Helmholtz instability occurs at the interface between two horizontal parallel fluid streams with different velocities and densities [N3-R1]. In contrast, Rayleigh-Taylor instability occurs when the lighter fluid is above the heavier fluid, and the current is less dense than the ambient [N3-R4]. The evidence further notes that Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities can arise in surface-propagating currents and can lead to mixing between the current and ambient fluid [N3-R3]. It also reports that Rayleigh-Taylor-like instabilities can emerge on top of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in certain configurations [N3-R5]. This indicates that the instability spectrum is not single-mode: the current may experience both shear-driven and buoyancy-driven instabilities simultaneously.

In experimental identification, onset is typically detected through the appearance of wave patterns, interface deformation, and the formation of mixing layers. The cited Kelvin-Helmholtz review states that the instability is identified at the interface between two streams with different velocities and densities [N3-R1]. The Rayleigh-Taylor instability is identified by the fact that it occurs when the lighter fluid is above the heavier fluid and the background is denser than the stream [N3-R2]. The surface-propagating current study specifically notes that mixing occurs via Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities during propagation, which is a clear experimental signature of instability onset [N3-R3]. The same evidence also indicates that Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities are associated with the formation of wave patterns and the breakdown of the interface into smaller structures [N3-R3]. The cited self-gravitating streams paper goes further by showing that instability growth is quantified through critical line mass, growth rates of shear layers, and the transition from turbulent shear penetration to gravitational fragmentation [N3-F3]. That study provides a quantitative experimental framework: instability is detected when the system crosses a critical line mass threshold, and the growth is then measured through the expansion of the shear layer and the resulting deceleration of the stream [N3-F3].

Growth rates and wave patterns are quantified using combinations of direct numerical simulations and analytical models, as well as observational measures. The cited paper on self-gravitating streams derives critical line mass as a function of Mach number and density contrast, and uses hydrodynamic simulations to measure the expansion rate of the turbulent shear layer [N3-F3]. It also reports that when gravity becomes important, penetration of the shear layer into the stream is halted by buoyancy forces, which allows quantification of how much the instability is suppressed by external stabilization [N3-F3]. For the Kelvin-Helmholtz case, the evidence implies that wave patterns are identified by the formation of bounded waves and the shape of the trough, which can be compared with theoretical or numerical predictions [N1-F1]. In the stratified ambient context, the cited study on planar gravity currents into a stratified ambient notes that internal gravity waves interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, and modify the shape of the current head [N4-F4]. This suggests that instability growth is quantified indirectly through changes in wave structure and head smoothing rather than through direct measurement of growth rates alone [N4-F4].

In short, the instability modes observed in less-dense-over-denser currents are Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities, with onset detected by interface deformation, wave formation, and mixing [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. Growth is quantified through critical thresholds, expansion rates, and wave pattern evolution, often supported by simulations and imaging [N3-F3][N1-F1][N4-F4].

Ambient and surface conditions significantly modify both spreading and stability in free-surface gravity currents. The most direct evidence is that ambient stratification can alter propagation speed, current shape, and the interaction between the current and the ambient fluid. The cited study on planar gravity currents into a stratified ambient states that ambient stratification introduces internal gravity waves that interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, decelerate current propagation, and smooth the current head [N4-F4]. This means that a denser, stratified ambient does not simply oppose the current passively; it actively changes the current’s kinematics by modifying wave dynamics and interface stability [N4-F4]. Another cited paper on gravity currents propagating into a stratified ambient similarly emphasizes that stratification modifies the current front velocity and that internal waves interact with the head [N4-R1]. The broader context from the same search result also notes that ambient stable stratification can reduce the sensitivity of gravity-current propagation to retarding effects, especially when the ambient is more strongly stratified [N4-R2]. This suggests that the effect of ambient stratification is not uniform: stronger stratification can either decelerate or weaken the influence of other retarding forces, depending on the balance of buoyancy and inertia [N4-R2].

Surface tension and evaporation are less directly emphasized in the provided evidence, but the general experimental context suggests that surface effects can influence current shape. The cited open-surface gravity-current paper discusses the measurement of free-surface depression modulated by the advancing current and the detection of bounded waves [N1-F1]. These effects are likely related to surface tension because the free surface is not fixed and can deform in response to the current’s motion. The same paper also notes that the open-surface case introduces a significant complication because the height of the upper boundary is variable in time and space [N1-F1]. This implies that surface effects can change the boundary condition of the flow and thus alter the current’s shape and propagation [N1-F1]. The evidence on reflected gravity currents adds another surface-related context: barriers can increase local turbulent mixing compared to horizontal surfaces, and image analysis is used to capture instantaneous density fields [N5-F2]. While this is not directly about surface tension or evaporation, it shows that surface geometry and the presence of barriers can strongly influence the current’s behavior through mixing and boundary interactions [N5-F2].

Initial conditions are another important determinant of instability development. The cited study on planar gravity currents into a stratified ambient notes that perturbations may alter the initial evolution of the current, especially when the gravity current is subcritical or slightly supercritical with small perturbations [N4-R5]. This indicates that the initial release configuration, including the strength of the current and the ambient stratification, can trigger or suppress instabilities [N4-R5]. The reflected-gravity-current study similarly emphasizes that the barrier’s geometry significantly affects mixing intensity and that barriers can increase local turbulent mixing [N5-F2]. This implies that initial conditions such as obstacle placement or barrier angle can influence the transition from laminar to unstable behavior [N5-F2]. In the broader gravity-current literature, the cited paper on lock-release systems also stresses that the presence of an open surface introduces a depression in the ambient fluid and that this effect is proportional to the density difference [N1-F1]. This suggests that even small changes in the initial density ratio or boundary condition can change the stability environment [N1-F1].

Overall, ambient stratification modifies spreading by altering propagation speed, wave interactions, and current-head shape [N4-F4][N4-R1]. Surface effects, while less explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, are important because the free surface can deform and affect boundary conditions [N1-F1]. Initial conditions, including the strength of the current, ambient stratification, and barrier geometry, strongly influence whether instabilities develop and how they evolve [N4-R5][N5-F2].

Experiments distinguish spreading from mixing primarily through separate observables that measure length-scale evolution and mixing intensity. The most relevant observables are interface length, width, buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, dissolution flux, and the ratio of mixing length to spreading length [N2-R3][N6-R3]. The cited study on mixing in stratified gravity currents specifically notes that high-resolution velocity and density measurements are used to determine the vertical flux of momentum and density, which is central to separating spreading from mixing [N6-R3]. This is important because spreading is often associated with the current’s outward length and thickness, while mixing is associated with the redistribution of momentum and density across the current’s width or depth [N6-R3].

Tracers, dyes, or flow visualization are used to infer mixing by revealing the structure of the current and the extent of interfacial deformation. The cited reflected-gravity-current study uses image analysis based on light attenuation to capture instantaneous density fields [N5-F2]. This is a form of flow visualization that helps identify where mixing occurs and how it is distributed in space. The same paper also notes that barriers can increase local turbulent mixing, and that the Thorpe scale is used to assess turbulent mixing intensity [N5-F2]. Thorpe-scale analysis is a standard way to quantify mixing intensity from density fluctuations, which makes it a useful experimental tool for distinguishing active mixing from passive spreading [N5-F2]. In the stratified-current context, the cited paper on mixing in stratified gravity currents emphasizes that high-resolution velocity and density measurements are used to determine mixing properties, supporting the idea that flow visualization and density measurements are complementary for separating mixing from spreading [N6-R3].

Mixing is quantified using mixing-length concepts, scalar dissipation rate, and turbulence intensity measures. The cited paper on mixing in stratified gravity currents reports the use of the Prandtl mixing length to describe the vertical flux of momentum and density [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This is a direct way to quantify mixing because the mixing length relates the rate at which momentum and density are exchanged across the current. The same paper also notes that in higher Reynolds numbers, mixing length increases and the relationship between flux and gradient becomes stronger, indicating that mixing is not just a binary on/off process but can vary continuously [N6-R1]. The reflected-gravity-current study adds that mixing intensity is assessed using the Thorpe scale, which is a quantitative measure of turbulent mixing from density fluctuations [N5-F2]. This supports the idea that mixing is treated as a separate effect when its intensity is measured independently of spreading length.

In practice, experiments treat mixing as a separate effect when it is not simply a consequence of spreading. The cited reflected-gravity-current study explicitly states that reflected flows are often simplified in theory as purely advective processes with no mixing, but experimental observations show that they involve much more complex behavior and significant mixing [N5-F2]. This is a key distinction: spreading can be measured as the outward growth of the current, while mixing is measured as the redistribution of density, momentum, or scalar quantities within the current. The evidence also shows that mixing can be triggered by obstacles, barriers, and initial conditions, and that its intensity depends on geometry and flow history [N5-F2]. This means that in experimental studies, mixing is often treated separately because it affects the current’s structure and dynamics in ways that are distinct from the spreading motion [N5-F2][N6-R3].

Overall, experiments distinguish spreading from mixing by measuring spreading length, thickness, interface length and width, buoyant mass, and scalar dissipation rate [N2-R3][N6-R3]. Tracers, dyes, and flow visualization are used to infer mixing structure, while mixing is quantified using the Prandtl mixing length, Thorpe scale, and scalar dissipation rate [N6-R1][N6-R2][N5-F2]. Mixing is treated as a separate effect when it is measured independently of spreading length and shown to contribute to turbulence and entrainment [N5-F2][N6-R3].

## Integrated explanation of how experiments characterize spreading behavior and instabilities of free-surface gravity currents

Experiments on free-surface gravity currents formed by less-dense water flowing over denser saline ambient water are designed to capture both the spreading behavior and the instability dynamics of these buoyancy-driven flows. Across the branch reports, the experimental approach is unified by a combination of controlled tank setups, high-resolution measurements, imaging, and quantitative observables. The goal is to track how the current spreads outward, how its shape evolves, and how instabilities develop and modify the flow. The evidence also shows that ambient stratification and surface effects can strongly influence both spreading and stability, while experiments routinely distinguish spreading from mixing using separate length-scale and mixing-intensity measures [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N6-R3][N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F4][N5-F2].

### 1) Experimental methods used to observe and quantify spreading behavior

The most common apparatus configurations in the branch reports are lock-release or lock-exchange tanks with open or free-surface boundaries, rather than fixed lids [N1-F1][N1-R1]. These setups are especially relevant for less-dense-over-denser currents because they allow the free surface to evolve dynamically and mimic natural and industrial flows [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence also points to a recent gravity-current setup operating at inflow Reynolds numbers around 4000, using different fluids to generate the current [N1-R4]. This indicates that experiments are not limited to simple rectangular tanks but can be tailored to specific flow regimes and Reynolds-number conditions.

To quantify spreading behavior, experiments measure velocity, thickness, and length scale using a variety of techniques. High-resolution velocity and density measurements are central to capturing the time-dependent evolution of the current [N6-R3]. In the spreading-length context, the branch report notes that observables such as buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, dissolution flux, and interface length and width are used to characterize spreading and mixing [N2-R3]. For length scales, the branch report also points to studies of spreading and leveling gravity currents in a Hele-Shaw cell, which is an analog for flows in narrow geometries [N2-R1]. This shows that spreading is analyzed not only through the overall outward growth of the current but also through spatially varying length and shape characteristics.

Thickness is usually inferred from the vertical extent of the current or from the interface between the two fluids. The branch report explicitly mentions accurate measurements of the space- and time-varying free-surface depression in experiments, which is a proxy for current height and thickness [N1-F1]. It also notes the detection of a bounded wave following the front, which helps validate models of the current’s vertical structure [N1-F1]. In the stratified ambient context, the branch report emphasizes that internal gravity waves interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, and modify the shape of the current head [N4-F4]. This indicates that thickness is often connected to the current’s head and the ambient stratification it encounters.

The free surface is tracked through imaging or sensor-based observation. The branch report states that image analysis is used to capture instantaneous density fields, and that light attenuation is used to visualize density variations [N5-F2]. This is a direct way to track the free surface and the interface between fluids. The same paper notes that non-intrusive techniques are used to capture density fields, which is important because intrusive sensors can perturb the flow [N5-F2]. In the open-surface gravity-current context, experiments are described as measuring the free-surface depression modulated by the advancing current, including the detection of bounded waves [N1-F1]. The reflected-gravity-current study also emphasizes image analysis as a method to reveal how barriers influence the current before impact [N5-F2]. Overall, imaging is not just a qualitative tool but a quantitative one, enabling the tracking of both surface position and density structure.

### 2) Instabilities observed and how they are identified experimentally

The main instability modes observed in less-dense-over-denser currents are Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and Rayleigh-Taylor instability, with Rayleigh-Taylor becoming especially relevant when the background fluid is denser than the current [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The branch report also notes that Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities can arise in surface-propagating currents and can lead to mixing between the current and ambient fluid [N3-R3]. It further reports that Rayleigh-Taylor-like instabilities can emerge on top of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in certain configurations [N3-R5]. This indicates that the instability spectrum is not single-mode: the current may experience both shear-driven and buoyancy-driven instabilities simultaneously.

In experimental identification, onset is typically detected through the appearance of wave patterns, interface deformation, and the formation of mixing layers. The branch report notes that Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is identified at the interface between two streams with different velocities and densities [N3-R1]. Rayleigh-Taylor instability is identified by the fact that it occurs when the lighter fluid is above the heavier fluid and the background is denser than the stream [N3-R2]. The surface-propagating current study specifically notes that mixing occurs via Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities during propagation, which is a clear experimental signature of instability onset [N3-R3]. The same evidence also indicates that Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities are associated with the formation of wave patterns and the breakdown of the interface into smaller structures [N3-R3].

Growth rates and wave patterns are quantified using combinations of direct numerical simulations and analytical models, as well as observational measures. The branch report cites a study on self-gravitating streams that derives critical line mass as a function of Mach number and density contrast, and uses hydrodynamic simulations to measure the expansion rate of the turbulent shear layer [N3-F3]. It also reports that when gravity becomes important, penetration of the shear layer into the stream is halted by buoyancy forces, which allows quantification of how much the instability is suppressed by external stabilization [N3-F3]. For the Kelvin-Helmholtz case, the evidence implies that wave patterns are identified by the formation of bounded waves and the shape of the trough, which can be compared with theoretical or numerical predictions [N1-F1]. In the stratified ambient context, the branch report notes that internal gravity waves interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, and modify the shape of the current head [N4-F4]. This suggests that instability growth is quantified indirectly through changes in wave structure and head smoothing rather than through direct measurement of growth rates alone [N4-F4].

### 3) How ambient and surface conditions modify spreading and stability

Ambient stratification has a major effect on current propagation and stability. The branch report states that ambient stratification introduces internal gravity waves that interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, decelerate current propagation, and smooth the current head [N4-F4]. It also notes that in a stratified ambient, internal waves interact with the head and modify the current front velocity [N4-R1]. The broader context from the same evidence further indicates that ambient stable stratification can reduce the sensitivity of gravity-current propagation to retarding effects, especially when the ambient is more strongly stratified [N4-R2]. This means that ambient stratification does not simply oppose the current passively; it actively changes the current’s kinematics by modifying wave dynamics and interface stability [N4-F4].

Surface effects are less directly emphasized in the branch reports, but the general experimental context suggests that they can influence current shape. The branch report notes that open-surface gravity-current experiments measure the free-surface depression modulated by the advancing current and detect bounded waves [N1-F1]. These effects are likely related to surface tension because the free surface is not fixed and can deform in response to the current’s motion. The same paper also states that the open-surface case introduces a significant complication because the height of the upper boundary is variable in time and space [N1-F1]. This implies that surface effects can change the boundary condition of the flow and thus alter the current’s shape and propagation [N1-F1]. The reflected-gravity-current study adds another surface-related context: barriers can increase local turbulent mixing compared to horizontal surfaces, and image analysis is used to capture instantaneous density fields [N5-F2]. While this is not directly about surface tension or evaporation, it shows that surface geometry and the presence of barriers can strongly influence the current’s behavior through mixing and boundary interactions [N5-F2].

Initial conditions are another important determinant of instability development. The branch report notes that perturbations may alter the initial evolution of the current, especially when the gravity current is subcritical or slightly supercritical with small perturbations [N4-R5]. This indicates that the initial release configuration, including the strength of the current and the ambient stratification, can trigger or suppress instabilities [N4-R5]. The reflected-gravity-current study similarly emphasizes that barriers can increase local turbulent mixing and that barriers significantly affect mixing intensity [N5-F2]. This implies that initial conditions such as obstacle placement or barrier angle can influence the transition from laminar to unstable behavior [N5-F2]. In the broader gravity-current literature, the branch report also notes that the presence of an open surface introduces a depression in the ambient fluid and that this effect is proportional to the density difference [N1-F1]. This suggests that even small changes in the initial density ratio or boundary condition can change the stability environment [N1-F1].

### 4) How experiments distinguish spreading from mixing

Experiments distinguish spreading from mixing primarily through separate observables that measure length-scale evolution and mixing intensity. The branch report identifies interface length, width, buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, dissolution flux, and the ratio of mixing length to spreading length as relevant observables [N2-R3][N6-R3]. The cited mixing-in-stratified-gravity-current study specifically notes that high-resolution velocity and density measurements are used to determine the vertical flux of momentum and density, which is central to separating spreading from mixing [N6-R3]. This is important because spreading is often associated with the current’s outward growth, while mixing is associated with the redistribution of momentum and density across the current’s width or depth [N6-R3].

Tracers, dyes, or flow visualization are used to infer mixing by revealing the structure of the current and the extent of interfacial deformation. The branch report notes that image analysis based on light attenuation is used to capture instantaneous density fields [N5-F2]. This is a form of flow visualization that helps identify where mixing occurs and how it is distributed in space. The same paper also notes that barriers can increase local turbulent mixing, and that the Thorpe scale is used to assess turbulent mixing intensity [N5-F2]. Thorpe-scale analysis is a standard way to quantify mixing intensity from density fluctuations, which makes it a useful experimental tool for distinguishing active mixing from passive spreading [N5-F2].

Mixing is quantified using mixing-length concepts, scalar dissipation rate, and turbulence intensity measures. The branch report cites a paper on mixing in stratified gravity currents that reports the use of the Prandtl mixing length to describe the vertical flux of momentum and density [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This is a direct way to quantify mixing because the mixing length relates the rate at which momentum and density are exchanged across the current. The same paper also notes that in higher Reynolds numbers, mixing length increases and the relationship between flux and gradient becomes stronger, indicating that mixing is not just a binary on/off process but can vary continuously [N6-R1]. The reflected-gravity-current study adds that mixing intensity is assessed using the Thorpe scale, which is a quantitative measure of turbulent mixing from density fluctuations [N5-F2]. This supports the idea that mixing is treated as a separate effect when its intensity is measured independently of spreading length [N5-F2].

In practice, experiments treat mixing as a separate effect when it is not simply a consequence of spreading. The branch report states that reflected flows are often simplified in theory as purely advective processes with no mixing, but experimental observations show that they involve much more complex behavior and significant mixing [N5-F2]. This is a key distinction: spreading can be measured as the outward growth of the current, while mixing is measured as the redistribution of density, momentum, or scalar quantities within the current. The evidence also shows that mixing can be triggered by obstacles, barriers, and initial conditions, and that its intensity depends on geometry and flow history [N5-F2]. This means that in experimental studies, mixing is often treated separately because it affects the current’s structure and dynamics in ways that are distinct from the spreading motion [N5-F2][N6-R3].

### 5) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports show that experiments on free-surface gravity currents formed by less-dense water over denser saline ambient water rely on a combination of controlled tank setups, high-resolution velocity and density measurements, imaging of density fields, and quantitative observables such as interface length, width, buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, and mixing length [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N6-R3][N2-R3][N5-F2]. They are designed to capture both spreading behavior and instability dynamics, with Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities being the most prominent instability modes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Ambient stratification can decelerate propagation, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, and smooth the current head, while surface effects and barrier geometry can influence current shape and mixing [N4-F4][N1-F1][N5-F2]. Experiments distinguish spreading from mixing by measuring separate length-scale and mixing-intensity observables, and mixing is quantified using the Prandtl mixing length, Thorpe scale, and scalar dissipation rate [N6-R1][N6-R2][N5-F2].

Overall, the experimental characterization of these currents is therefore a multi-layered process: tracking the free surface and the current’s evolution, identifying instability onset and growth, quantifying ambient and surface effects, and separating spreading from mixing using distinct observables [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F4][N6-R3][N5-F2].

The main instability modes observed in less-dense-over-denser currents are Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and Rayleigh-Taylor instability, with Rayleigh-Taylor becoming especially relevant when the background fluid is denser than the current [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The branch report also notes that Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities can arise in surface-propagating currents and can lead to mixing between the current and ambient fluid [N3-R3]. It further reports that Rayleigh-Taylor-like instabilities can emerge on top of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in certain configurations [N3-R5]. This indicates that the instability spectrum is not single-mode: the current may experience both shear-driven and buoyancy-driven instabilities simultaneously.

In experimental identification, onset is typically detected through the appearance of wave patterns, interface deformation, and the formation of mixing layers. The branch report notes that Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is identified at the interface between two streams with different velocities and densities [N3-R1]. Rayleigh-Taylor instability is identified by the fact that it occurs when the lighter fluid is above the heavier fluid and the background is denser than the stream [N3-R2]. The surface-propagating current study specifically notes that mixing occurs via Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities during propagation, which is a clear experimental signature of instability onset [N3-R3]. The same evidence also indicates that Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities are associated with the formation of wave patterns and the breakdown of the interface into smaller structures [N3-R3].

Growth rates and wave patterns are quantified using combinations of direct numerical simulations and analytical models, as well as observational measures. The branch report cites a study on self-gravitating streams that derives critical line mass as a function of Mach number and density contrast, and uses hydrodynamic simulations to measure the expansion rate of the turbulent shear layer [N3-F3]. It also reports that when gravity becomes important, penetration of the shear layer into the stream is halted by buoyancy forces, which allows quantification of how much the instability is suppressed by external stabilization [N3-F3]. For the Kelvin-Helmholtz case, the evidence implies that wave patterns are identified by the formation of bounded waves and the shape of the trough, which can be compared with theoretical or numerical predictions [N1-F1]. In the stratified ambient context, the branch report notes that internal gravity waves interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, and modify the shape of the current head [N4-F4]. This suggests that instability growth is quantified indirectly through changes in wave structure and head smoothing rather than through direct measurement of growth rates alone [N4-F4].

### 3) How ambient and surface conditions modify spreading and stability

Ambient stratification has a major effect on current propagation and stability. The branch report states that ambient stratification introduces internal gravity waves that interact with the current head, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, decelerate current propagation, and smooth the current head [N4-F4]. It also notes that in a stratified ambient, internal waves interact with the head and modify the current front velocity [N4-R1]. The broader context from the same evidence further indicates that ambient stable stratification can reduce the sensitivity of gravity-current propagation to retarding effects, especially when the ambient is more strongly stratified [N4-R2]. This means that ambient stratification does not simply oppose the current passively; it actively changes the current’s kinematics by modifying wave dynamics and interface stability [N4-F4].

Surface effects are less directly emphasized in the branch reports, but the general experimental context suggests that they can influence current shape. The branch report notes that open-surface gravity-current experiments measure the free-surface depression modulated by the advancing current and detect bounded waves [N1-F1]. These effects are likely related to surface tension because the free surface is not fixed and can deform in response to the current’s motion. The same paper also states that the open-surface case introduces a significant complication because the height of the upper boundary is variable in time and space [N1-F1]. This implies that surface effects can change the boundary condition of the flow and thus alter the current’s shape and propagation [N1-F1]. The reflected-gravity-current study adds another surface-related context: barriers can increase local turbulent mixing compared to horizontal surfaces, and image analysis is used to capture instantaneous density fields [N5-F2]. While this is not directly about surface tension or evaporation, it shows that surface geometry and the presence of barriers can strongly influence the current’s behavior through mixing and boundary interactions [N5-F2].

Initial conditions are another important determinant of instability development. The branch report notes that perturbations may alter the initial evolution of the current, especially when the gravity current is subcritical or slightly supercritical with small perturbations [N4-R5]. This indicates that the initial release configuration, including the strength of the current and the ambient stratification, can trigger or suppress instabilities [N4-R5]. The reflected-gravity-current study similarly emphasizes that barriers can increase local turbulent mixing and that barriers significantly affect mixing intensity [N5-F2]. This implies that initial conditions such as obstacle placement or barrier angle can influence the transition from laminar to unstable behavior [N5-F2]. In the broader gravity-current literature, the branch report also notes that the presence of an open surface introduces a depression in the ambient fluid and that this effect is proportional to the density difference [N1-F1]. This suggests that even small changes in the initial density ratio or boundary condition can change the stability environment [N1-F1].

### 4) How experiments distinguish spreading from mixing

Experiments distinguish spreading from mixing primarily through separate observables that measure length-scale evolution and mixing intensity. The branch report identifies interface length, width, buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, dissolution flux, and the ratio of mixing length to spreading length as relevant observables [N2-R3][N6-R3]. The cited mixing-in-stratified-gravity-current study specifically notes that high-resolution velocity and density measurements are used to determine the vertical flux of momentum and density, which is central to separating spreading from mixing [N6-R3]. This is important because spreading is often associated with the current’s outward growth, while mixing is associated with the redistribution of momentum and density across the current’s width or depth [N6-R3].

Tracers, dyes, or flow visualization are used to infer mixing by revealing the structure of the current and the extent of interfacial deformation. The branch report notes that image analysis based on light attenuation is used to capture instantaneous density fields [N5-F2]. This is a form of flow visualization that helps identify where mixing occurs and how it is distributed in space. The same paper also notes that barriers can increase local turbulent mixing, and that the Thorpe scale is used to assess turbulent mixing intensity [N5-F2]. Thorpe-scale analysis is a standard way to quantify mixing intensity from density fluctuations, which makes it a useful experimental tool for distinguishing active mixing from passive spreading [N5-F2].

Mixing is quantified using mixing-length concepts, scalar dissipation rate, and turbulence intensity measures. The branch report cites a paper on mixing in stratified gravity currents that reports the use of the Prandtl mixing length to describe the vertical flux of momentum and density [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This is a direct way to quantify mixing because the mixing length relates the rate at which momentum and density are exchanged across the current. The same paper also notes that in higher Reynolds numbers, mixing length increases and the relationship between flux and gradient becomes stronger, indicating that mixing is not just a binary on/off process but can vary continuously [N6-R1]. The reflected-gravity-current study adds that mixing intensity is assessed using the Thorpe scale, which is a quantitative measure of turbulent mixing from density fluctuations [N5-F2]. This supports the idea that mixing is treated as a separate effect when its intensity is measured independently of spreading length [N5-F2].

In practice, experiments treat mixing as a separate effect when it is not simply a consequence of spreading. The branch report states that reflected flows are often simplified in theory as purely advective processes with no mixing, but experimental observations show that they involve much more complex behavior and significant mixing [N5-F2]. This is a key distinction: spreading can be measured as the outward growth of the current, while mixing is measured as the redistribution of density, momentum, or scalar quantities within the current. The evidence also shows that mixing can be triggered by obstacles, barriers, and initial conditions, and that its intensity depends on geometry and flow history [N5-F2]. This means that in experimental studies, mixing is often treated separately because it affects the current’s structure and dynamics in ways that are distinct from the spreading motion [N5-F2][N6-R3].

### 5) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports show that experiments on free-surface gravity currents formed by less-dense water over denser saline ambient water rely on a combination of controlled tank setups, high-resolution velocity and density measurements, imaging of density fields, and quantitative observables such as interface length, width, buoyant mass, scalar dissipation rate, and mixing length [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N6-R3][N2-R3][N5-F2]. They are designed to capture both spreading behavior and instability dynamics, with Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities being the most prominent instability modes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Ambient stratification can decelerate propagation, inhibit Kelvin-Helmholtz billows, and smooth the current head, while surface effects and barrier geometry can influence current shape and mixing [N4-F4][N1-F1][N5-F2]. Experiments distinguish spreading from mixing by measuring separate length-scale and mixing-intensity observables, and mixing is quantified using the Prandtl mixing length, Thorpe scale, and scalar dissipation rate [N6-R1][N6-R2][N5-F2].

Overall, the experimental characterization of these currents is therefore a multi-layered process: tracking the free surface and the current’s evolution, identifying instability onset and growth, quantifying ambient and surface effects, and separating spreading from mixing using distinct observables [N1-F1][N1-R1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F4][N6-R3][N5-F2].
